_meta.purpose: G2 commit-accuracy evaluation: per-fallacy reference examples (good + bad) to measure LLM output fidelity. Backend's post-check validates generated examples against this gold set.
_meta.scoring: For each generated example: (1) check for name-leak via aliases.json (automatic rejection if found), (2) does it genuinely exemplify the fallacy (human or heuristic eval), (3) does it avoid false positives (e.g., a true-cause example that happens to discuss causation shouldn't fail the false-cause test). G2 target: ≥90% commit-accuracy, zero name-leaks.

good_examples: array of 2-3 known-good reference texts that clearly exemplify the fallacy, no name-leak
bad_examples: array of 1-2 texts that look plausible but don't actually exemplify this fallacy — used to tune false-positive rejection thresholds

good_examples: After Will argued we should invest more in healthcare, Warren said that clearly Will wants to bankrupt the country by throwing unlimited money at every problem.
When Sarah proposed a carbon tax on industry, Tom responded that she wanted to shut down all manufacturing and throw workers into poverty.
The senator claimed that funding education would solve poverty. His opponent countered that this idea is absurd because it assumes money alone fixes every social problem.
bad_examples: Will argues healthcare spending should rise. Warren thinks that's wasteful. They disagree on the facts, not on what the other person said.
Sarah proposed a specific carbon tax rate. Tom said the rate she chose is too aggressive. This is a factual disagreement, not a misrepresentation of her argument.

good_examples: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths both spike in summer. Therefore, ice cream must cause drowning.
Ever since my company adopted a new software tool, revenue has grown 15%. The tool caused the growth, not the market expansion that happened at the same time.
Roosters crow at dawn, and the sun rises. So roosters cause sunrise.
bad_examples: Factory emissions increased while air quality declined. This is a genuine causal relationship supported by evidence.
Symptoms worsened after I stopped taking my medication. In this case, causation is clearly established by the mechanism of action.

good_examples: Think of starving children in poor countries! How can you argue for cutting international aid? (Using guilt/pity in place of evidence.)
Everyone you love will die horribly of disease if you don't vote for my candidate! (Fear-mongering without addressing the candidate's actual record.)
My opponent is a pedophile. Don't you care about protecting children? (Character attack with inflammatory language, no substantive argument.)
bad_examples: Workplace safety regulations save lives, and people deserve dignity at work. These are reasoned claims supported by moral and practical arguments.
Climate change threatens coastal cities and ecosystems. This statement conveys a genuine risk based on evidence, not just emotional manipulation.

good_examples: Jane argues that aliens visit Earth because UFOs are unexplained. That argument is fallacious. Therefore, aliens definitely don't visit Earth.
My opponent's evidence is anecdotal, which is fallacious reasoning. So his conclusion must be wrong — even though the conclusion could be true for other reasons.
The company's marketing uses an appeal to emotion. So their product must be useless. (The product could still be genuinely good despite bad marketing.)
bad_examples: Your argument contains a logical flaw, and your conclusion is also false. This can be coincidentally true without committing the fallacy.
The evidence you cited is weak, so I'm skeptical of your claim. Skepticism based on poor evidence is reasonable.

good_examples: If we allow same-sex marriage, next we'll be forced to accept marrying pets and family members. (No causal mechanism; pure speculation.)
Legalizing marijuana will inevitably lead to heroin legalization and the collapse of society. (Extreme hypothetical with no intermediate steps.)
Allowing remote work one day a week means the office will vanish entirely and companies will fail.
bad_examples: Smoking often leads to lung cancer. This is a real causal chain with evidence.
Poverty can lead to desperation and increased crime rates. This is a plausible causal sequence based on research.

good_examples: You're stupid and ugly, so your opinion on economics is wrong. (Attacking the person, not the argument.)
She's a former addict, so we shouldn't trust her analysis of addiction policy. (Character assassination instead of engaging with the substance.)
He's a divorced man, so his views on marriage are worthless. (Personal trait used to dismiss the argument itself.)
bad_examples: You made a logical error in your reasoning, so your conclusion is questionable. (Critique of the argument, not the person.)
This economist's track record on forecasts is poor, so I'm doubtful of this prediction. (Relevant expertise assessment.)

good_examples: You criticized me for lying, but you also lied last week! So your criticism is invalid.
My opponent says I should raise taxes on the wealthy. I respond by pointing out that he also owns investments and pays low tax rates — so he's a hypocrite and his argument is wrong.
You say I cheat at games. But you cheated too! So you have no right to accuse me.
bad_examples: You say honesty is important, but I've never seen you lie. Your argument stands on its own merits.
You criticize my research methods. Those methods are actually sound, and your critique misunderstands the study design. (Defending the argument itself.)

good_examples: I don't understand how evolution could produce consciousness from simple cells, so evolution must be false.
Quantum mechanics seems weird and counterintuitive to me, so the theory must be wrong.
I can't imagine how artificial intelligence could write poetry, so large language models can't really be intelligent.
bad_examples: The math behind quantum entanglement is complex. I'll study it more deeply to understand it.
This theory seems counterintuitive, so I want to review the evidence carefully. (Legitimate scientific inquiry.)

good_examples: Astrology failed every scientific test, but that's only because scientists have a closed mind. They don't have faith!
My psychic powers never show up under controlled conditions, but that's because the test is too rigid and inhibits my abilities.
I said all swans are white. You found a black swan, but that one doesn't count — it's not a 'true' swan.
bad_examples: This drug failed Phase 1 trials in healthy subjects but may work in disease populations. This is a reasonable distinction.
My hypothesis doesn't apply to this edge case for legitimate reasons documented in my paper. (Scientific caveat.)

good_examples: When did you stop beating your wife? (Presupposes guilt of beating.)
Have you finally become honest? (Presupposes a history of dishonesty.)
Don't you think global warming is a Chinese hoax? (Presupposes it is a hoax.)
bad_examples: Did you attend the meeting yesterday? (Straightforward factual question.)
What is your position on climate policy? (Open-ended, no hidden assumption.)

good_examples: I claim there's a teapot orbiting Mars. You can't prove me wrong, so my claim is true.
Unicorns exist. Prove they don't. If you can't, I win the argument.
I have telepathic powers. Since you can't disprove it, you must believe me.
bad_examples: Scientists must prove their theories with experiments and data. (Correct burden of proof.)
Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. (Appropriate calibration of proof burden.)

good_examples: The sign said 'Fine for parking here,' so I naturally assumed it was fine to park.
The law says no vehicle may enter the park. I drove my toy car through it and claimed the law doesn't apply because it's not a real vehicle.
Bank capital is invested in stocks. Capital punishment should be invested in stocks too! (Exploiting 'capital' having two meanings.)
bad_examples: The term 'depression' in psychology means something different from the economic definition. This distinction is important for clarity.
The word 'lead' has multiple meanings, so I need to specify whether I'm discussing the metal or the verb. (Legitimate disambiguation.)

good_examples: I've lost five hands of poker in a row, so I'm due to win the next hand.
Red came up on the roulette wheel four times in a row. Black is now very likely on the next spin.
My lottery ticket numbers haven't won in 10 years, so they're more likely to win this time.
bad_examples: This weighted die favors odd numbers, so over 1000 rolls, odd will appear more. (Accurate statistical reasoning.)
If the lottery is fair, each number has equal probability every draw. (Correct understanding of probability.)

good_examples: Everyone believes in astrology, so it must be true.
Most people think this movie is great, so you should too.
Millions follow this influencer, so their medical advice must be sound.
bad_examples: Many scientists agree on the theory of gravity. This agreement is based on evidence and experiments.
A majority of voters support this policy. This reflects their democratic choice, not necessarily evidence of correctness.

good_examples: A celebrity said this diet works, so it must be safe and effective, even though the celebrity has no medical training.
This famous actor thinks vaccines are harmful. Therefore, vaccines are harmful. (No medical expertise.)
A TV personality claims quantum physics proves telepathy. Since he's on TV, it must be true.
bad_examples: A peer-reviewed study by leading physicists in the field concludes X. This is credible due to their expertise and the process.
A cardiac surgeon advises me on heart health. Their professional training makes this relevant.

good_examples: Atoms are invisible. Humans are made of atoms. Therefore, humans must be invisible.
Every part of a piano is lightweight. So a piano is lightweight. (False: the whole piano is heavy.)
The team is undefeated. So each player is undefeated in every sport they play. (False: composition doesn't always work.)
bad_examples: The team is composed of Olympic athletes. The team likely has strong athletic performance. (Reasonable inference.)
Water molecules consist of hydrogen and oxygen. Water can be broken down into hydrogen and oxygen. (Factually accurate.)

good_examples: No Scotsman puts sugar on his porridge. My neighbor is Scottish and puts sugar on porridge. Then he's not a *true* Scotsman!
A true capitalist would never advocate for regulation. If someone advocates for regulation, they're not a true capitalist. (Definitional retreat.)
A real conservative always opposes government spending. My conservative friend supports infrastructure spending. So he's not a real conservative.
bad_examples: By definition, a triangle has three sides. A four-sided figure is not a triangle. (Proper definition.)
A democracy requires free elections. A country with rigged elections is not a true democracy. (Meaningful distinction based on criteria.)

good_examples: This idea comes from a disreputable source, so it must be wrong. (Ignoring the merit of the idea itself.)
You grew up in a poor neighborhood, so your opinions on economics are invalid.
This research was funded by Big Oil, so the conclusions are lies. (Ignoring the actual methodology and results.)
bad_examples: This research was funded by Big Oil. Let me examine the methodology carefully to see if bias occurred. (Warranted skepticism.)
His religious background influences his worldview. Understanding his background helps me contextualize his arguments. (Valid context.)

good_examples: You're either with us or against us. (False dichotomy; there are other positions.)
Either vaccines are 100% safe or they're completely dangerous. (False: nuanced risk-benefit analysis needed.)
You either love your country or you criticize its government. (False: patriotism can include critique.)
bad_examples: This light switch is either on or off. (Legitimate dichotomy.)
A statement is either true or false. (Appropriate binary for truth values.)

good_examples: God must exist because the Bible says so, and the Bible is the word of God.
This medicine works because it's effective. (Conclusion restates the premise.)
Violence in video games is harmful because it's bad for you.
bad_examples: Smoking causes lung cancer. Studies show a mechanism and correlation. (Supported by evidence.)
Gravity pulls objects down. This is explained by mass and spacetime curvature. (Supported by physics.)

good_examples: This medicine is natural, so it's safe and effective. (Hemlock is natural but deadly.)
Homosexuality is unnatural, so it's wrong. (Appeals to nature as moral standard without evidence.)
Humans are naturally competitive, so cooperation is futile. (Nature ≠ moral guide.)
bad_examples: This herb has been used in traditional medicine for centuries and now research confirms benefits. (Nature + evidence.)
Humans naturally feel empathy, which is why moral systems often emphasize compassion. (Describing natural tendency, not justifying morality.)

good_examples: My grandfather smoked 30 cigarettes a day and lived to 97, so smoking isn't dangerous.
I tried this diet and lost 10 pounds, so it works for everyone.
My friend took this supplement and got better, so it must cure the disease. (Ignoring statistics on recovery rates.)
bad_examples: Controlled studies show this medication is effective in 80% of cases. Here's my personal experience consistent with that data.
Surveys of 10,000 people indicate this trend. My own observation aligns with the broader pattern. (Anecdote + data.)

good_examples: I found three countries where Sugarette drinks are popular AND healthy. So Sugarette causes health! (Ignoring the hundreds of other countries.)
These five days had unusually high stock gains. I'll build a trading strategy around these specific days. (Pattern from noise.)
I noticed that my headaches started after I switched detergent. So the detergent causes headaches. (Correlation from selective observation.)
bad_examples: Controlled studies tracked 100 people over 2 years and found a consistent pattern of headaches after detergent exposure. (Systematic research.)
Multiple independent studies replicate the relationship between X and Y, suggesting a real phenomenon. (Convergent evidence.)

good_examples: Vaccines cause autism vs. vaccines are safe. The truth is vaccines cause some autism but not all. (False: the claim is entirely disproven.)
The Earth is flat vs. the Earth is round. Compromise: the Earth is slightly bumpy. (Both poles are wrong, no middle ground.)
We should have 0% or 100% government. Compromise: 50% government. (Arbitrary compromise on an unrelated scale.)
bad_examples: Free market vs. regulated market. A mixed economy may balance both benefits.
Strict discipline vs. permissive parenting. Research suggests moderate, consistent approach may be effective. (Genuine middle position.)
